body:
Meaning of the Chalcolithic Age

The term Chalcolithic combines the idea of copper with that of stone. It refers to cultures in which people used copper objects alongside stone implements. The Chalcolithic Age is therefore also called the Copper–Stone Age.

Copper could be shaped into tools and ornaments. However, stone tools remained important because stone was often more readily available and suitable for particular cutting, scraping and grinding activities. The adoption of copper did not mean that every implement in a settlement was made from metal.

Chalcolithic culture: A culture characterised by the combined use of copper and stone technology, usually identified together with other features such as settlement patterns, pottery and subsistence activities.

Copper, Bronze and Iron Are Not the Same

Copper is a metal. Bronze is an alloy, commonly produced by combining copper with tin. Iron is a different metal that became widely important in many Indian regions at a later stage.

The use of copper alone is not sufficient to classify a settlement as an Iron Age site. Equally, the use of copper does not automatically indicate that a community possessed the full urban organisation of the Harappan civilisation.

Settlement and Housing

Many regional Chalcolithic communities lived in villages or smaller farming settlements. Houses could be circular, square or rectangular. Common construction materials included mud, sun-dried mud-bricks, wooden posts, reeds and thatch.

Some walls were made using wattle and daub: a framework of branches or reeds was covered with mud to form a wall. Houses often contained hearths and storage spaces. Larger settlements sometimes included substantial buildings or protective walls, but these were not universal features.

How Chalcolithic People Obtained Food

Most important regional Chalcolithic cultures of western and central India combined crop cultivation with animal husbandry. Wheat, barley, pulses, millets and, in suitable environments, rice were among the crops cultivated at different sites. Cattle, sheep, goats and other animals were reared.

Hunting, fishing and collecting wild foods continued to supplement village diets. Crop choices depended on local rainfall, soil and growing conditions. Therefore, a settlement in Rajasthan need not have followed exactly the same agricultural pattern as a village in Maharashtra.

Pottery and Regional Identity

Pottery is one of the most recognisable features of regional Chalcolithic cultures. Both handmade and wheel-made pottery occurred, with wheel-made vessels important at many sites. Potters produced storage jars, cooking vessels, bowls, dishes and specialised shapes such as spouted pots.

Different cultures developed characteristic combinations of clay colour, surface treatment and painted decoration. These differences help distinguish Ahar–Banas, Kayatha, Malwa and Jorwe cultures. The same broad colour description, however, can occur in different periods: Black and Red Ware, for example, is not exclusive to one culture or to the Iron Age.

Crafts and Exchange

Village economies also included toolmaking, pottery production, beadmaking and other crafts. Some sites have yielded beads of semiprecious stones, copper ornaments and evidence of specialised production.

The distribution of particular materials and artefacts indicates that settlements sometimes obtained resources or finished objects from beyond their immediate surroundings. Such exchange could connect neighbouring villages and more distant regions. It does not follow that every regional Chalcolithic culture was part of one centrally organised economic system.

Relationship with Harappan Civilisation

The Harappan civilisation developed major urban centres, including planned settlements, craft-production areas and long-distance exchange networks. Several non-Harappan Chalcolithic cultures existed during overlapping periods but had their own regional pottery and settlement patterns.

The correct distinction is therefore between a technological description, such as copper–stone use, and a particular cultural or urban tradition, such as the Harappan civilisation. They are not interchangeable labels.

Prelims focus

  • Chalcolithic means Copper–Stone Age.
  • Copper and stone implements were used together.
  • Bronze is an alloy commonly made from copper and tin.
  • Important regional Chalcolithic cultures include Ahar–Banas, Kayatha, Malwa and Jorwe.
  • Wattle and daub means a framework of branches or reeds covered with mud.
  • Trap: Every Chalcolithic village was not a Harappan city.

[INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 27, Chalcolithic Cultures Northern and Central India, sections 2–6, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Module 28, Chalcolithic Cultures of Western India, sections on chronology, pottery, subsistence and settlement, consulted 17 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, printed pp. 32–42, 2018–19 text.]

title: The Chalcolithic Age: Copper–Stone Technology and Village Economies

body:
Regional Cultures and Their Importance

During the Chalcolithic period, several farming and pastoral communities developed distinct regional traditions. Three especially important traditions for preliminary examinations are Ahar–Banas in Rajasthan, Kayatha in Madhya Pradesh and Malwa in central India.

Their identification depends on a combination of location, settlement features, pottery styles and material culture. Their dates overlap in some areas, and a single site may preserve remains from more than one tradition.

The Ahar–Banas Culture

The Ahar–Banas culture developed mainly in the Mewar region of southeastern Rajasthan, especially around the Banas River and associated valleys. Important sites include Ahar, near Udaipur, Gilund and Balathal.

The characteristic pottery association is Black and Red Ware decorated with white-painted designs, although several other pottery types also occur. The white painting is an especially useful recognition feature in objective questions.

Communities cultivated cereals and pulses and kept animals such as cattle, sheep and goats. Houses, hearths and storage facilities indicate an established village economy. Copper objects were used alongside stone tools.

The Ahar–Banas tradition has a long chronology. At Balathal, dated material places its Chalcolithic occupation broadly between about 3700 BCE and 1830 BCE. These dates describe the archaeological sequence identified at that site and should not be treated as identical beginning and ending dates for every Ahar–Banas settlement.

The Kayatha Culture

The Kayatha culture is associated primarily with the Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh, especially areas connected with the Chambal river system. Kayatha is its principal named site, and cultural remains have also been found at Dangwada.

A distinctive pottery type is Chocolate-slipped Ware, sometimes bearing painted designs. Other pottery varieties include buff ware with red painting and combed ware.

Kayatha settlements used copper axes and ornaments as well as stone tools. Agriculture and the keeping of domesticated animals formed part of the economy. The culture is commonly placed around 2000–1800 BCE, although precise dates depend on the evidence from individual sites.

The Malwa Culture

The Malwa culture was important in the river valleys of western and central Madhya Pradesh, including areas connected with the Narmada, Chambal and Betwa systems. Major sites include Navdatoli, Nagda and Eran.

Navdatoli, on the Narmada River, is particularly important for its settlement remains. Malwa communities lived in structures made from combinations of mud, wood and other local materials. They cultivated cereals and pulses, kept domestic animals and made stone and copper implements.

The characteristic Malwa Ware usually has a buff or cream-coloured surface with dark brown or black-painted designs. Painted motifs could be geometric or represent plants, animals and people.

A commonly used date range for the Malwa Chalcolithic phase in Madhya Pradesh is approximately 1700–1500 BCE. The Malwa cultural tradition also occurs in Maharashtra, where its local chronological position differs. Inamgaon is an important example of a Deccan settlement with a Malwa phase followed by Jorwe phases.

Culture–Site–Pottery Comparison

CultureMain regionImportant sitesCharacteristic pottery
Ahar–BanasSoutheastern RajasthanAhar, Gilund, BalathalBlack and Red Ware, often painted in white
KayathaMalwa region, Madhya PradeshKayatha, DangwadaChocolate-slipped Ware
MalwaMadhya Pradesh; also Deccan phasesNavdatoli, Nagda, EranBuff or cream ware with dark painting

Ahar–Banas: Rajasthan and white-painted Black and Red Ware. Kayatha: Madhya Pradesh and Chocolate-slipped Ware. Malwa: Navdatoli and cream or buff pottery with dark-painted designs.

Why the Traditions Should Not Be Confused

A pottery colour alone is sometimes insufficient for identification because different traditions could use related manufacturing methods. More reliable recognition comes from combining the pottery description with the site and its regional setting.

Similarly, a settlement can have successive occupations. The discovery of Malwa cultural material at Inamgaon does not make every subsequent occupation of Inamgaon part of the Malwa culture.

Prelims focus

  • Ahar–Banas is associated with Mewar in Rajasthan.
  • Ahar, Gilund and Balathal are important Ahar–Banas sites.
  • Kayatha is associated with Madhya Pradesh and Chocolate-slipped Ware.
  • Navdatoli is a major Malwa site on the Narmada River.
  • Malwa Ware commonly has a buff or cream surface with dark-painted designs.
  • Trap: Malwa occupation at Inamgaon preceded its important Jorwe phases.

[INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 27, Chalcolithic Cultures Northern and Central India, sections 2, 4, 5 and 6, consulted 17 November 2026; INFLIBNET, Module 28, Chalcolithic Cultures of Western India, sections on chronology and the Inamgaon sequence, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Ahar–Banas, Kayatha and Malwa: Major Chalcolithic Cultures of India

body:
The Chalcolithic Cultures of Maharashtra

The Deccan region of present-day Maharashtra had several Chalcolithic traditions. Important named phases include Savalda, local Malwa phases and Jorwe. Settlements were often situated near rivers, cultivable land and sources of pasture.

Important archaeological sites include Jorwe, Inamgaon, Nevasa, Prakash and Daimabad. Some of these sites preserve more than one cultural phase and cannot be assigned exclusively to one tradition.

Jorwe Pottery and Technology

The Jorwe culture takes its name from the site of Jorwe in Maharashtra. Its characteristic pottery is generally red or orange-red ware with black-painted designs. Important vessel forms include spouted pots and carinated bowls. A carinated bowl has a distinct angular change in the shape of its sides.

Jorwe communities used copper objects but continued to rely on stone blades, grinding stones and other implements. Pottery production, beadmaking and other crafts formed part of the economy.

Early and Late Jorwe Phases

A commonly used archaeological chronology for the Deccan places the Early Jorwe phase around 1400–1000 BCE and the Late Jorwe phase around 1000–700 BCE. These are broad regional dates rather than exact boundaries for every settlement.

Early Jorwe settlements in parts of Maharashtra show substantial houses, organised food production and well-made decorated pottery. In several places, later occupation was smaller or changed in character. Inamgaon is important because it preserves evidence of these developments over a long period.

Inamgaon: Location and Settlement

Inamgaon is located in present-day Maharashtra on the Ghod River, a tributary of the Bhima. Its occupation extended broadly from the 2nd millennium BCE into the early 1st millennium BCE, with Malwa and Jorwe phases.

Excavations revealed houses, hearths, storage facilities, pottery, plant remains and animal bones. These show a mixed village economy combining cultivation, herding and the use of wild resources.

Crops included wheat, barley, pulses and millets. Animal remains include cattle, sheep and goats, along with several wild species. Such evidence is important because a Chalcolithic village was not simply an agricultural field with houses: it was a community engaged in several forms of production and food collection.

Burial Practices at Inamgaon

Inamgaon is particularly notable for its burials. Children were often buried in earthen urns; a characteristic arrangement involved 2 urns placed mouth-to-mouth. Some burials occurred within residential areas or below house floors.

One especially unusual burial contained a man placed in a 4-legged clay jar in a cross-legged position. It was found in the courtyard of a substantial 5-roomed house near a granary. The exceptional burial and the size of the associated structure suggest that the individual may have held high social status. His precise identity or office cannot be established as a certainty.

Inamgaon is a Chalcolithic site, not a standard example of a megalithic stone-cist burial. Its exceptional 4-legged jar burial must not be confused with the stone chambers and stone-circle markers characteristic of many megalithic graves.

Changes in the Later Jorwe Economy

At Inamgaon, the Late Jorwe phase shows changes in housing, pottery and food production. Compared with the earlier phase, some dwellings were smaller or more simply constructed, and fine painted pottery became less common.

Animal remains suggest a reduced emphasis on cattle and a greater relative importance of sheep, goats and some wild animals. Crops and collected foods also changed. These shifts are consistent with increased pressure on the settlement economy.

Several Chalcolithic settlements in Maharashtra were abandoned or substantially reduced around the later phases. Drier conditions, resource pressure and changing subsistence strategies may have contributed. However, a single definite cause for the decline of all settlements cannot be established.

Prelims focus

  • Jorwe is a Chalcolithic culture strongly associated with Maharashtra.
  • Jorwe Ware generally has black-painted designs on a red or orange-red surface.
  • Inamgaon lies on the Ghod River, a tributary of the Bhima.
  • Inamgaon contains Malwa and Jorwe cultural phases.
  • Child burials at Inamgaon commonly included mouth-to-mouth double urns.
  • Trap: The exceptional 4-legged jar burial does not prove the identity of the deceased as a chief.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 5, What Books and Burials Tell Us, printed pp. 49–50, 2018–19 text; INFLIBNET, Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, Module 28, Chalcolithic Cultures of Western India, sections 2, 5, 7 and 8, including A Case Study—Inamgaon, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: The Jorwe Culture and Inamgaon: Chalcolithic Life in the Deccan
